items.title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
items.author: Jeremy Hsu
items.content: The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment. “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10. items.title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
items.author: Andrea Griffiths
items.content: How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline. An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database. I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills”. Define one job and when it applies A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With Proof Agent, we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose: --- name: proof-agent description: Adversarial verification of AI-generated work. Spawns an independent verifier to check for false claims, broken code, and security issues. --- At the center is a simple rule: self-verification is not verification. The When to Verify section in Proof Agent’s SKILL.md says when to invoke the skill. The remaining instructions explain what the verifier reviews and what evidence to include in its findings. Coordinate multiple skills for a larger workflow When the judgment that makes a data pipeline correct lives in four different people’s heads, those four people are the roadmap. Each change to the pipeline depends on their availability and knowledge of the data. Data Forge is an example of how to capture parts of that judgment in skills that work together. In the support-desk pipeline example, we start with a request for metrics that count incidents created and resolved. Before building the pipeline, the forge-init skill discovers details such as source tables and naming conventions, then writes them to a resolved manifest. The other skills read that manifest for the project context they need. The forge-builder skill then coordinates the work from the issue through to a pull request. It uses forge-dbx to query the data platform and forge-lint to apply the team’s standards as it designs and builds the pipeline. A person reviews the proposed decisions along the way, and the resulting pull request contains the pipeline code, schema changes, and tests. Each skill has a defined responsibility, and they share project context instead of rediscovering it independently. When a step changes, you can change one skill and leave the rest alone. Skills fit bounded, repeatable work that benefits from reusable judgment, such as a checklist, release, migration, or metric pipeline. If a workflow needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail, long-running control, or permissions enforced outside the model, an application is a better fit. Keep project configuration out of the skill We don’t want to hardcode every project’s names, database, or conventions into the skills. In the Data Forge support-desk example, a manifest describes the project, metric store, and platform so the skills can use the right project details without baking them into their instructions: project: name: "support-desk" store_name: "support_metric_store" platform: engine: "duckdb" pipeline_framework: "spark_python" duckdb_dir: "warehouse" With the discovered details in the resolved manifest, the other skills don’t have to make their own assumptions about the project. Keep discovered project details separate from team standards. The forge-init initialization skill can inspect existing schemas and code patterns; the forge-lint skill supplies the rules to follow before code is generated. A pattern found in a repository isn’t automatically a rule to preserve, so make discovered details reviewable and let people confirm or change them where business judgment is needed. To check portability, ask: could another team use these skills with its own manifest without rewriting them? Share execution paths between skills The forge-dbx skill gives the other Data Forge skills one way to access the data platform. It reads the manifest and selects a Databricks or DuckDB adapter, so each skill doesn’t need its own connection and query logic. The manifest can choose DuckDB for the local support-desk demo, but it can’t install the DuckDB CLI or grant database access. Those remain setup responsibilities for the environment and its user. The manifest picks the engine; the host provides the access. Put checks and approval points in the workflow The Data Forge support-desk workflow has seven phases, with a human checkpoint at each one. The workflow overview shows how the skills fit together. Before a phase proceeds, the workflow checks that the previous phase is complete; before schema changes run, it asks for approval. The Proof Agent example applies the same principle to code review. A GitHub Actions workflow gives the verifier the original request and code changes, but not the coding agent’s own assessment. The verifier returns PASS, FAIL, or PARTIAL and must cite evidence in the changed files. The GitHub Action does a static review of the diff; it doesn’t execute code or run tests. In the demo workflow, we set block-on-fail: false so findings were advisory. By default, a FAIL fails the check, which blocks the merge if the check is required. The aim is to keep test results and merge requirements in your repository’s CI checks and rules. Package for each agent client, then verify its setup Supporting multiple clients can mean keeping several copies of the same instructions in sync. In the Data Forge example, we keep skills/*/SKILL.md as the source and use a packaging script to generate client-specific files: .claude-plugin/plugin.json for Claude Code, .cursor-plugin/plugin.json for Cursor, and .github/agents/*.agent.md for GitHub Copilot. The script also includes a check mode for CI: node scripts/package.mjs --check Clients can differ in their available models, tools, credentials, and permissions. After installing a skill, check that the client recognizes it for the intended task, loads its references, can use the required tools, and returns the evidence the skill calls for. Three practices for building agent skills Put business context in one file. Keep project-specific names, schemas, and conventions in a manifest, and have each skill read it instead of duplicating those facts. This gives the team one visible place to update configuration. Give related skills one consistent way to use the platform. Have related skills use the same path to run queries, jobs, and schema changes instead of each defining its own commands and connection logic. This makes the workflow’s access easier to understand and its behavior easier to check in each client. Use instructions to guide the work, and checks to verify it. A skill can tell an agent which standards to follow and when to ask for approval. Add human review at decisions that need context or judgment, and use tests and CI checks to catch issues before a change moves forward. If a check must block a merge or deployment, configure that requirement in your repository’s rules. Start with the task you’re tired of explaining. Write down what it needs, where it stops, and what a reviewer sees. Then try it with another agent and improve it as you learn what works. Add an agent skill to GitHub Copilot > The post Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: llm-gemini 0.37
items.content: Release: llm-gemini 0.37 Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family. It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme: Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Hydrogen $1.50 $0.075 $7.50 Carbon and Argon are the same price, and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task. Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that. I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans. Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels: Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark. Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models: In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows. Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search. Tags: gemini, llm, google, pelican-riding-a-bicycle, llm-pricing, ai, llms

items.title: In reversal, American Cancer Society urges routine prostate cancer screening
items.author: Beth Mole
items.content: In a significant update to its guidelines for prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society is now recommending that men get routinely screened for prostate cancer with a PSA test. Men at average risk should get a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69, according to the new guidelines released Thursday. Men considered at high risk due to race and family history should start testing earlier, at 45, and most are recommended to get tested every year. Specifically, yearly testing starting at age 45 is recommended for all Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer. Non-Black men should also get yearly testing starting at 45 if a close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or if more than one of their relatives has had prostate cancer. On the other hand, if only one close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer and it was diagnosed at age 65 or older, non-Black men in this case should start PSA screening at 45, but are recommended to get testing only every two years. items.title: GitHub availability report: October 2026
items.author: Jakub Oleksy
items.content: We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability. The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery. As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity. That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range. We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm. We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%. Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow. The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery. The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features. October 05 19:11 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 38 minutes) Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes. Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features. What went wrong and why? Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted. Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs. How did we respond? A partial networking failure began, and actions jobs started backing up. Alerts flagged errors and slow job assignment, and we declared an incident. We redeployed the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners, but it did not recover. We traced the failures to the networking issue. We failed over the affected databases and storage to healthy regions, one service at a time, and added capacity. Actions recovered, but some other affected services kept failing even after failover. We worked with our cloud provider to resolve the networking failure. The remaining services recovered, and we resolved the incident. How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? We are making the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners better able to handle sudden increases in load, so it keeps up when another region shifts extra jobs to it. We now have expanded prioritization of runner assignment based on customer profile when available runner capacity is degraded. We are changing the behavior of GitHub-hosted runners to reduce recovery time when job assignment services are degraded for a period of time. We are improving how quickly we detect and locate partial network failures between our datacenters and the cloud-hosted services they depend on. October 06 19:57 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 43 minutes) Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused. Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request. Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed. What went wrong and why? A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests. The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released. To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches. How did we respond? A surge of migration work overloaded a shared database, causing requests across github.com to fail or slow down. Automated monitoring detected the failures and paged our on-call engineers. The errors stopped on their own within minutes. We declared an incident and paused enterprise migrations to prevent a recurrence while we investigated the cause. Once a mitigation was deployed, we resumed migrations and resolved the incident. How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? We optimized the query GitHub Enterprise Importer sends to the database so that each one stays small and fixed in size. We are automating importer backoff when the database is under strain, easing load before it can affect other GitHub services. We are adding database alerts that flag queries doing much more work than usual and identify which query is responsible, so we can find and fix problems like this one faster. October 07 15:14 and 17:17 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 11 minutes, and 47 minutes, respectively) Duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause. Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery. Web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages. What went wrong and why? During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again. How did we respond? Automated monitoring alerted us to failing writes, and we declared an incident. Writes recovered when an established machine with correct records became leader and published correct settings. We traced the cause to the new machine, resolved the first incident, and paused automated maintenance to prevent a repeat. When a maintenance task did not honor the pause and the outage repeated, we declared a second incident. Writes recovered when an established machine became leader again. We removed the new machine and resolved the second incident. How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? We improved how we retire database servers, so outdated records aren’t left behind. We tightened controls on adding new machines that manage database routing, and making sure automated maintenance honors a pause. We strengthened validation of database routing settings, so incorrect settings are caught before they take effect. October 19 15:49 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 7 minutes) Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes. Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded. What went wrong and why? An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link. How did we respond? Automated alerts detected the failures, we declared an incident, and we traced the problem to the shared network link. We routed the actions service away from some of its cache servers in that region, but the link was still over capacity. We routed it away from the rest of those cache servers, and the link recovered. We raised processing limits to clear the actions backlog, and we resolved the incident once all affected services had recovered. How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? We have limited how quickly this actions service can open new connections to its cache servers. We are alerting on spikes in new connections from this service to identify and address the source sooner. October 21 14:52 UTC (lasting 4 hours and 30 minutes) Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes. Customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, new commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours. Audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes. Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered. What went wrong and why? Some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, new connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers. We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the issue. Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear. How did we respond? We declared an incident and moved some traffic off an overloaded server, but more servers became overloaded soon after. We split the busiest traffic into more partitions and moved it to less-loaded servers. All affected features except audit logs gradually recovered. Once the audit log service stopped restarting, we raised the rate at which it could write events so the backlog would clear faster. We resolved the incident once audit log delays were back within the healthy range, and the remaining backlog cleared afterward. How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? We added randomized delays to reconnects after a failed request, so servers that are already slow don’t get hit with a burst of new connections. We are alerting earlier on server memory use, so we can move traffic before a server slows down. We are adding a second destination for webhook delivery data that we can switch to, so we can keep webhook deliveries moving if our event streaming platform slows down. We have improved our playbooks to move hot partitions for similar situations in the future October 28 14:12 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 16 minutes) Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes. Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model. Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily. What went wrong and why? Copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time. How did we respond? A credential we use with an upstream model provider stopped working, and requests to the affected models began to fail. Alerts flagged rising errors on the affected models, and we declared an incident. We posted a public status update and recommended choosing another model in the meantime. We traced the errors to our own credential and created a replacement. We began deploying the new credential, and requests started to recover once the first environment was updated. We completed the deployment in the remaining environments, confirmed that requests to the affected models had recovered, and resolved the incident. How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? We improved how our service handles authentication failures from upstream model providers, so requests can be retried instead of failing. We are strengthening how we manage credentials for upstream model providers. We are adding alerts for authentication failures from upstream model providers, so we can identify and address this kind of problem faster. October 30 14:31 UTC (lasting 31 minutes) Duration: approximately 9 minutes. Customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Issues, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors. What went wrong and why? A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. New requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed. The pool was already running near capacity when some update requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over. How did we respond? Requests used up every connection in the shared database pool, and requests across github.com began to fail. We declared an incident after seeing failures, and on-call engineers for the affected services were paged. The pool drained and error rates returned to normal. Shortly after, we confirmed that the full connection pool had caused the errors and posted a public status update. We verified that database connections were back to normal and resolved the incident after monitoring for stability. How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? We are now running the slow lookup before these update requests start writing a change, so they no longer hold a database connection while they wait. We are evaluating limits on how long a pooled database connection can be held, so a slow request pattern is less likely to tie up the pool. Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog. The post GitHub availability report: October 2026 appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: AI Ambition: ArtCraft Cloned Photoshop and Now Wants to "Rebuild Everything"
items.author: Richard MacManus
items.content: The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI. And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools, starting with a Photoshop alternative built from scratch in Rust called PhotoCraft. You could feel the excitement in the room this morning when ArtCraft founder and CEO Brandon Thomas presented a kind of manifesto for AI-based open source at AIE Code. When he mentioned that ArtCraft had cloned Adobe’s Acrobat, with a product called PdfCraft, it got a round of applause from the audience. In wrapping up, his rallying cries of “let's take back the entire internet” and “let's rebuild everything” were greeted with whoops and cheers. Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream. “We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.” His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.” When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody into the fold.” Thomas acknowledged that this widened the scope of internet software, but at the cost of that freedom to build with leading apps. “The diffuse, experimental, early web started to disappear,” he said. “The APIs got taken away from us, and then we started seeing distribution being gatekept by the big providers.” It seems Adobe in particular annoyed Thomas. He described getting billed with an unexpected fee when he cancelled a monthly plan. “It's really frustrating that the web — that was once really, really promising and open and free — has turned into this extractive, owned, rent-seeking world.” This inspired him to start ArtCraft, “with the ethos of ‘let's build everything open source.’” A message even anti-AI people have gotten behind, according to Thomas. In addition to PhotoCraft, they’ve copied other apps in the Adobe suite, cloned Figma, and created a Microsoft-like word processor called WordCraft. There are also independent apps such as SolidCraft, a community-led CAD project distributed through ArtCraft’s launcher. Thomas reiterated that these AI-built applications are 100% open — “not only the desktop apps, but the actual infrastructure as well.” PhotoCraft: The development process ArtCraft is starting with rewriting familiar tools. Thomas’s longer-term vision is for users (such as artists who were previously using Photoshop) to tailor the software to their own workflows. As he framed it, they want to “undo what had happened during Web 2.0, when everything became owned and consolidated and gatekept, and just give people back their applications.” AI is the means to achieve that, he said. But aren’t there already open source alternatives to Photoshop, like GIMP? “GIMP isn't really used by artists,” said Thomas during his presentation. “We actually observed artists vibe coding their own workflows on top of the software that we gave them.” To begin creating PhotoCraft, the team gave an AI model a detailed prompt outlining Photoshop’s tools, data structures and file importers. After that, they “laid out a large, large prompt to say, let's build out the application.” As part of that process, they made everything MCP and CLI compatible. Within 24 hours, said Thomas, “we were looking at a pretty good approximation of what Photoshop was — and it kind of blew our minds away.” PhotoCraft interface; via ArtCraft website Thomas noted that PhotoCraft is “still not at 100% parity” — he said they’ve just passed 60% — but the team has set an internal goal to reach as close to 100% as possible. (The project’s GitHub claims about 76% parity for feature breadth and about 46% for professional readiness.) “Right now, we want to fill the muscle memory of all the artists that use Adobe. So we are going for Adobe, their interface and ‘look and feel’ directly.” But after ArtCraft has achieved that, they plan to “build new apps that have new interfaces that are more agentic.” A big reaction Thomas said he was surprised by the amount of attention PhotoCraft, in particular, has gotten — ranging from the New York Times requesting an interview, to a swelling of its open source community to about 4,000 developers. “I'm still struggling to bear with what has happened. It struck a nerve with people. They felt sort of maligned by Adobe and other tech companies. And what we built has really resonated with them.” After his presentation, Thomas was mobbed by AIE Code attendees. ArtCraft’s apps are being downloaded at the rate of about 1.7 million per day, which Thomas said is still accelerating. In addition to the 17 official apps, there are around 300 being developed by the community, he added. Rust is key, but there have been technical challenges Other than the AI technology, Thomas said that Rust was a crucial part of making the apps performant — he claimed that PhotoCraft opens ten times faster than Photoshop, for example. “Rust was probably essential in this product's success,” he said. “We've seen people do it in Electron before, but for high-quality creative apps, you really need something that's native.” For those engineers who are not experts in Rust, Thomas has good news for you. “Do you need to know Rust to start using Rust today as an engineer? Definitely not. [...] Your agents will drive it just fine.” However, Thomas admitted that not everything has gone swimmingly. “We've run into a lot of gotchas — like permissions, GitHub, scaling, CI,” he said. “CI is falling over. We've been spinning up our own. We found a good place to get RAM on co-located servers.” But they have found an equilibrium on what agents can do and what needs to be handled by people. “If you're doing backend work or things that require schema migrations [or] API design, let your humans do that. But for desktop apps and games and anything that's basically immutable, throw your agents at it and give them full confidence.” And it turns out, there’s even an ArtCraft solution for you there. “AutoCraft is a completely autonomous software factory that we're going to open source.” AI open source FTW There’s no doubting the ambition of Brandon Thomas and his ArtCraft company. “We can open source the entire world,” he proclaimed at the end of his presentation. “Let's own our apps, our infra, our protocols, our models — all of it.” It’s a big vision, potentially even on the scale of Linux if its current downloads growth rate continues. But, ironically perhaps, what intrigues me most about ArtCraft is the growth of its human contributor community. After all, that’s what the original web got most right: human collaboration at scale. The big difference from the 1990s is that now it’s agents doing the bulk of the development work.
